Closure commences by first moving the microscope out of the surgical field. The 
dura is closed in a watertight fashion with the aid of the temporalis fascia graft using 
a 4-0 suture (Fig. 4.1n). The craniotomy defect is then covered with a titanium mesh 
plate, which is held in place with screws (Fig. 4.1o). The wound is then copiously 
irrigated with bacitracin-containing saline. The muscle, fascia, and galea are subse-
quently closed in layers with interrupted 2-0 braided polyglactin sutures (Fig. 4.1p). 
The skin is closed with a 3-0 polypropylene running suture (Fig. 4.1q). A sterile 
dressing is finally applied after the head is taken out of the three-pin head holder.

Closure
Theprimarygoal in closureis isolation of thesubarachnoid space
from the extradural compartment and eliminating any open
connection to the air cells of the temporal bone. An excellent
material to achieve these goals is adipose tissue. An adipose graft is
harvested from the lower abdomen. The tissue is cut into thin strips
for placement in the defect (see Video 3, showing dural opening,
tumor removal, and closure). Whether closing after a middle fossa
approach or extended approach, the method of laying strips of
adipose tissue into the fenestration in the temporal bone is the
same. Each strip is laid across the floor of the middle fossa with its

Introduction
Vestibular schwannomas (VS) are benign, extra-axial, encapsulated, Schwann cell 
derived neoplasms of the vestibular part of the eighth cranial nerve. Although some 
earlier reports indicated that the superior vestibular nerve is the more common ori-
gin of VS, recent studies suggest otherwise. Sanna et al. found that the most com-
mon origin for VS are the nerve sheath of the inferior vestibular nerve, and less 
frequently the superior vestibular nerve [1]. Eighth cranial nerve schwannomas rep-
resent 90% of all intracranial nerve sheath tumors [2]. VS account for approxi-
mately 6–8% of intracranial tumors in adults [3, 4] and are the most common tumor 
in the cerebellopontine angle (CPA) ranging between 80% and 95% [5, 6], followed 
by meningiomas ranging between 5% and 10% and epidermoid tumors ranging 
between 4% and 7% [7–9]. There are two types of VS; sporadic and familial. The

Additionally, facial nerve tumors often involve multiple segments with the most 
common being the geniculate ganglion and demonstrate enhancement on MRI or 
bony changes to the fallopian canal beyond what can be expected for primary VS [60, 
61, 63, 64]. However, in lesions that resemble primary VS (facial nerve schwanno-
mas limited to the IAC and CPA), the symptom profile is typically indistinguishable 
from primary VS with typically no evidence of facial nerve dysfunction [58, 59]. 
Often, the intraoperative clue that the surgeon has encountered a primary facial nerve 
lesion is that there is no tissue plane between the lesion and the facial nerve. The 
entire substance of the lesion will often stimulate with the facial nerve stimulating 
electrode. Sometimes, with small or medially based lesions, the facial nerve can be 
traced medially from the meatal foramen and the lesion and nerve become one entity.

This case is presented to demonstrate difficulties inherent with large multi-cystic 
VSs. Cystic vestibular schwannomas are notorious for being adherent to both neural 
and vascular structures, poor outcomes, and sudden growth and expansion. These 
features make cystic VS cases quite challenging. When dealing with such cases, 
these points should be taken into consideration: (1) When manipulating the cystic 
part of the tumor it is important not to break the cyst wall, which may be quite thin 
in some portions, since this may result in losing the surgeons ability to handle of the 
cyst wall. (2) There are often small brainstem arteries adherent to the cyst wall.

Facial Nerve Anatomy
The FN can be divided into the following segments: brainstem, cisternal, canalicu-
lar/meatal, labyrinthine, geniculate ganglion, tympanic, mastoid, extratemporal. 
Typically, unless a massive or erosive lesion is encountered (extremely rare), the 
tympanic, mastoid, and extratemporal portions of the nerve are not encountered in 
surgical management of VSs. Additionally, the nerve has two main roots: the motor 
root and a root known as the nervous intermedius.

Seventh and eighth nerves originate from the lateral aspect of the brainstem, 
traverse CPA cistern and IAC terminate in the inner ear, where they provide 
innervation of the vestibular end organs. The CPA cistern is an expansion of the 
subarachnoid space between the lateral lobe of the cerebellum, cerebellar 
peduncles, and lateral pons medially and the temporal bone laterally. In the far 
lateral IAC, CoN enters the modiolus of the cochlea at the cochlear aperture, FN 
enters the meatal foramen to become the labyrinthine segment of FN, and the 
SVN & IVN enter the labyrinth of the inner ear. Chorda tympani nerve enters

Molecular Biology of Vestibular Schwannoma
The neurofibromin 2 gene is located on chromosome 22 (22q12) and produces a cell 
membrane-related protein known as merlin or schwannomin. This end-product of 
the NF2 gene is a tumor suppressor protein. Biallelic dysfunction of NF2 gene 
induces neoplastic transformation and thus results in tumor development. Both VS 
and NF2 syndrome have a close pathophysiological relationship which is linked to 
the disruption of the NF2 gene. The unilateral VS are sporadic whereas bilateral
